# INTRODUCTION

## Overview

The Ministry of Education (MOE) is responsible for education in Malaysia and is putting emphasis on modernizing education in Malaysia under the Malaysia Education Blueprint 2013-2025. In this blueprint, according to the MOE (2013), one focus is the integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) to enhance the standard of education and the efficiency of administration work.

Sekolah Rendah Islam Al Amin Wilayah Persekutuan (SRIAAWP) is a private Islamic school which plays an important role in the school sector since it offers specialized and value-based education. These are the ones that work as a big ecosystem that deals with things such as academic curricular and parental involvement. To maintain operational quality, efficient management is important especially due to the scale of these activities.

In this kind of setting, the ability to manage information seamlessly is important to ensuring the success of the institution. Guan (2021) states that an efficient administrative system can enable schools to centralze workflows, like student record-keeping and resource coordination. Saaida (2023) noted that these tasks can be streamlined, which can help staff to minimize manual tasks and better focus their efforts on providing a quality education.

## Problem Background

SRIAAWP’s manual workflow processes causes numerous operational issues. To start with, currently SRIAAWP faces significant information silos, where important school data is scattered across multiple platforms. This leads to the inorganization of data management within the school.

Furthermore, teachers and staff of SRIAAWP rely on fragmented Google Drive folders for curriculum, student affairs, and co-curricular management. This causes inefficience administration with the lack of an administrative hub.

Moreover, parents of children who study in SRIAAWP are overwhelmed by a flood of messages across numerous Telegram groups provided by the school. This leads to difficulty in retrieving specific event details due to the lack of structure like a calendar (Takwim) format.

Lastly, student information are recorded manually, with the lack of a central platform to store their information like their co-curricular achievements. This causes strain to the teachers in charge when trying to retrieve any relevant information about the student.

## Project Aim

The aim of the project is to develop the AI Integrated School Portal using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) for SRIAAWP to solve the identified operational needs.

## Project Objectives

The objectives of the project are:

To analyze the requirements of the administrative and communication requirements of the stakeholder, SRIAAWP.

To design and develop a centralized web application for SRIAAWP including an administrative dashboard integrated with AI- powered RAG for teachers and an information dashboard integrated using a conflict-free calendar for parents.

To test the system’s usability using User Acceptance Testing (UAT), User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ) and other suitable testing techniques.

## Project Scope

The scopes of the project are:

Focus on developing a web application, including an administrative hub integrating an AI assistant chatbot for querying school documents and an automated conflict checker for event scheduling.

The project will be implemented in two semesters with the stakeholder being SRIAAWP and the target users being teachers, parents, and students.

## Project Importance

This web application is a significant importance to the staffs at SRIAAWP, and also the individual parents that are involved. Benefits like reducing the unnecessary resources used to sift through scattered information and saving time by providing an AI chatbot assistant that can give instant support (Saaida, 2023). SRIAAWP’s teachers can eliminate human error and enhance objectivity with the automation (Baijun, 2024) of current manual workflow like the event scheduling using the conflict-based calendar. In addition, the student information stored will avoid being outdated due to being linked with the system, which will automate updates depending on the staff in charge.

## Report Organization

This thesis is separated into six organized chapters. Firstly, Chapter 1 Introduction gives the general overview of the SRIAAWP Portal including the problems it is trying to solve. Moving on to Chapter 2 Literature Review, reviews currently existing technologies and explains the technology used in developing the system. Chapter 3 System Development Methodology covers the methodology used throughout the development lifecycle following the standard Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). Furthermore, Chapter 4 Requirement Analysis and Design will present the requirements gathered, the architecture of the system, the User Interface (UI), and also the data structure of the system. Chapter 5 Implementation and Testing will cover the documentation of the testing and implementation of the system. Lastly, Chapter 6 Conclusion will summarize this Final Year Project 1 (FYP1) project’s results.

# LITERATURE REVIEW

## Introduction

This chapter describes the foundation for building the SRIAAWP Portal System. It begins by defining the problem domain through a SRIAAWP case study to find the primary requirements established during a recent interview. This serves as the starting point for SRIAAWP’s shift towards a digital system.

A detailed look at the current manual operations at SRIAAWP is carried out with an in-depth talk given by the stakeholder. The chapter also offers a specific literature review on the technology stack, focusing on the chosen frameworks, coding tools, and database options to ensure all technical choices follow modern software engineering standards.

## Case Study

SRIAAWP carries out its primary operations in Taman Sri Rampai, Kuala Lumpur while being part of the broader SRI Al Amin network of private schools (Al-amin.edu.my, 2026). SRIAAWP aims to provide high quality academic education while also maintaining their deep Islamic values and instilling them into their students, however their operational workflow highly affects and obstructs their efficiency because of their lack of digitization and reliance on manual processes. Up to 25% of employees’ time of work in the day are spent just searching for internal information (Chui et al., 2012). The analysis of SRIAAWP’s organization is necessary to understand the requirements and problems encountered.

### School Organization Structure

SRIAAWP’s organization is built on 1 headmaster, 3 department manager and 9 senior teachers. Sir Mohamad Faiz bin Azizan is the headmaster with the assistance of Madam Nurul Fatehah binti Rosehaizan, Madam Zainab bt. Musa and Madam Asm’a binti Wan Sukri, as the department managers. These departments consist of Curriculum, Student Affairs and Extra curriculum (Co-curriculum) departments, and have senior teachers in their respective departments. ## Current System Analysis

Figure . Swimlane Diagram for Current SRIAAWP Memo Notification Workflow

Figure 2.2 shows the processes involved in the current operational workflow of document management and info notification at SRIAAWP. It is sequential and involves three main actors which are Admin/Department Head, teachers, and parents. This process relies heavily on manual intervention across disconnected platforms.

The workflow begins when the admin or department head starts the process by preparing a document/memo or meeting minutes. Once a document is finalized, the administrator uploads the file to the Google Drive folder for long-term record keeping while at the same time, informing the teachers under their respective department through forwarding the information to the teachers’ group on Telegram.

Following that, teachers serve as the middle layer in this communication sequence. Upon receiving notification via Telegram, teachers must manually update their personal class records if the information isn’t needed at the current time. However, if the teacher needs to find the information after some time has passed, they would have to manually sift through the multiple Google Drive folders and documents to retrieve the desired information. Once the relevant information is located, the teachers then must manually forward the data to their respective Telegram class groups.

The parents, being the end-users of this information, experience the most hindrance within the current system. Information is delivered to parents inside the high volume Telegram class groups, and whether it is structured or not depends on how the teachers constructed it. After receiving the information, parents will read the information and forget it after a while if the information is not needed at the current time. However, if the parents needs to find the information at one point in time, they would have to scroll through extensive chat histories to find the specific information.

Figure . Swimlane Diagram for Current SRIAAWP Takwim Coordination

Figure 2.3 shows the current workflow for the annual takwim drafting and finalization. This process includes three actors which are the Admins/Department Heads, teachers and parents. The process starts with the admin/department head drafting the annual takwim in a table management software like Excel, and exporting it to a PDF or image file type. Once saved, the document is uploaded into the Google Drive for long term use. A decision is made where if an event date has been changed or rescheduled, the admin would need to re-draft the annual takwim again, and repeat the previous process. However, if no event date has been changed, then the admin proceeds to broadcast the draft to all the telegram groups.

Following the broadcast of the annual takwim, the teachers are then informed to make sure there are no clashes or mistakes made by the admins. If the teachers have a new event ideas they would like to hold, they would have to check if the event date of said event clashes with the current takwim. If it does, they would have to inform the adminstrators about the conflict, however if no conflict is found, they can proceed with the events.

As for the parents’ side, after receiving the notification of the annual takwim in the Telegram group, they then have a choice depending on whether they need the information currently or not. If not, they would at a high probability forget the dates and soon will once again ask the teachers for  the information in the Telegram groups. However, if they do need the information, they can add the dates of events to their personal calendar.

Figure 2.3 Swimlane Diagram for Current SRIAAWP Co-Curricular Activity

Figure 2.3 shows the current workflow for the co-curricular activity including retrieving achievement information and updating new achievement submissions. This process include 2 main actors which are the teachers, and the students. The process starts if the students wants to retrieve their co-curricular achievements records, and also if they want to submit new achievements from external sources. If they choose to, they then need to ask their respective teachers about the information and wait for some response.

Following that, if the teacher in charge receives information from the students, that they want to submit a new submission, the teachers would then have to review the submission, to ensure that they follow the standard school co-curricular requirements. After revision, the teachers will then need to manually update their personal records of the students. After that, they would have to inform their students about the successful submission. Finally, the students will receive the information, and their records will have been updated.

## Comparison between existing systems

The required digitalized solution should address the complicated operational requests, such as centralized documentation management, public access of school related information, easily viewable School Calendar (Takwim), and an trackable achievements for students in the form of a dashboard. To justify the need for the proposed solution and to determine the most appropriate technological basis, a comparison between existing systems is essential.

We will compare the capabilities of IMuslehMelaka (IMUSLEHMELAKA.EDU.MY., 2024) and E-SMART SMUAAUK (E-SMART SMUAAUK PLATFORM, 2026), which represents the competition.

Table 2.1	Comparison of Attribute between IMuslehMelaka and E-SMART SMUAAUK

| Attribute | E-SMART SMUAAUK | IMuslehMelaka |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accessibility of School Calendar | Not set to public view (Information about events is not accessible) | No School Calendar (Lacks structure for information) |
| Documentation Management | Heavily relies on Google Drive to store documents | No centralized management |
| AI-Integration | Lacks any modern AI assistant | Lacks any modern AI assistant |

Table 2.1 evaluates the three distinct attributes of solutions against the two primary competitors. The attributes focuses on accessibility of information, internal management and modernized AI assistance. These systems lack any centralized management, and some sort of structure in their information, causing strain for staff and users outside of their organization.

## Literature Review of Technology Used

The development of a modern and scalable web-based school portal covers the development environment, frontend framework, information management, and backend infrastructure. Visual Studio Code (VSCode) is widely considered the standard Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for any web application development. It is able to support the frontend framework of Next.js that uses React’s UI Library with TypeScript language, that also comes with a lot of features and optimizations built in (Venkata, Karu Lal, Harshith and Sreekanth, 2021). Due to IDE support, TypeScript enables a 23% faster fix in bug-fixing tasks, and provides substantial improvements in code quality, such as a 38% fewer security vulnerability (Kuznetsova and Cherkasov, 2025).

When talking about the backend manager, Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS) has become the modern standard to increase the speed of development, because the developers can focus on the development of the front-end features (Dudjak & Martinović, 2020, p. 208). One commonly used BaaS in the current landscape is Supabase, which is an open source BaaS platform built on top of PostgreSQL (Supabase, n.d.).

# SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT METHODOLOGY

## Introduction

This chapter outlines the structured and iterative development approach undertaken to build the SRIAAWP School Management and Communication Portal, designed specifically for the administration management at SRIAAWP. This system was developed to facilitate a centralized administration management hub, automate event management, provide a centre of information regarding the school, and digitalize student’s achievements for better management.  To ensure a structured and organised development cycle, the project has adopted the Waterfall Agile Hybrid methodology, which enables careful planning, clear and structured documentation, while also making sure of rapid feedback from stakeholders, and incremental delivery of functional components (Kavuru, 2024). This chapter explains on the rationale behind choosing Hybrid methodology, describes the phases of the development strategy, and discusses how the selected technologies were progressively integrated in alignment with the evolving system requirements.

## Methodology Choice and Justification

The Waterfall-Agile hybrid methodology was selected for the SRIAAWP School Management and Communication project because this approach has great chemistry in projects that require both the structured planning side and the flexibility side of software development. With the combination of Agile’s adaptability and Waterfall’s predictability, the development of this project can handle evolving requirements while still adhering to deadlines and regulations (Luca, 2022). This works well with the way the Final Year Project (FYP) 1 and FYP 2 course is structured, where FYP 1 focuses on the requirements analysis and extensive documentation, while FYP 2 focuses primarily on the development and testing of the system (PSM Committee, 2014).

While pure waterfall approach operates on the principle of sequential and detailed planning, this causes some downsides and makes it challenging to incorporate changes after the initial scope has been approved. Changes are treated as undesirable events, and requires re-evaluating schedules and deliverables, thus this rigidity limits the response to unforeseen changes, potentially causing delays or reworks (Bastos, Pierott, Navarro, Tam, Najjar and Haddad, 2025). That being said however, although pure agile approach embraces change as an expected and desirable element throughout the development cycle, it can also hinder long-term maintenance because of the nature of it neglecting documentation and its challenges in managing physical product iterations (Leech and Hanslo, 2025).

Moving on, it is understandable as to why this project chooses the hybrid approach as it takes the intermediate stance. In general, phases managed using an agile approach is more readily accepting to changes, while still remaining tightly controlled in stages that follow traditional approach (Bastos et al., 2025). Furthermore, one incredibly significant benefit of the hybrid approach is its ability to mitigate risks through identifying and correcting issues earlier in development. This is done through waterfall’s structured planning which ensures compliance requirements are met upfront, while agile’s iterative operations allows developers to address emerging risks and respond to changing conditions swiftly (Luca, 2022).

## Phases of the Chosen Methodology

The development of the SRIAAWP School Management and Communication project followed a structured Waterfall-Agile hybrid methodology, broken down into multiple general phases. A general portrayal of the Waterfall-Agile-Approach (WAA) is shown in Figure 3.1 below.

Figure 3.1 Waterfall-Agile-Approach (Prenner, Unger-Windeler and Schneider, 2020, p. 150)

Commonly, projects using the WAA method, uses the waterfall model as the base methodology. According to Prenner et al (2020), there are six general phases that are closely similar to Royce’s description of the waterfall model. The first phase is the requirements analysis phase, where the business needs and overall requirements for the system are analyzed. Next, in the design phase, the approach is followed by the creation of the general architecture for the system. Liskin (2015) states that during the first phase, the requirements are often documented in different artifacts, and these artifacts are then transformed into a product backlog. This is followed by the iterative implementation phase, where agile methods are used, and detailed requirements along with design decisions are made. After implementation, verification tests are conducted at the testing phase, and later the product is released during the operations phase (Prenner et al, 2020).

### Gantt Chart and Phases Description

Figure 3.2 Gantt chart showing the timeline for each phase

Figure 3.2.1 Gantt chart left side (Zoomed in)

Figure 3.2.2 Gantt chart right side (Zoomed in)

The figure shown above shows the Gantt chart for this project’s timeline. As stated previously, the WAA consists of six phases, and these phases are incorporated throughout the development of this project.

**Requirements Analysis and Documentation Preparation Phase**. In this phase, the business requirement for the product is analyzed, the vision for the project is formulated, and the business assumptions and constraints are discussed (Prenner et al, 2020). Extensive meetings with stakeholders are held to remove ambiguities in the requirements and needs set. Following that, proper structured documentations are made throughout the waterfall methodology. Prenner et al (2020) states that this phase aims to elicit the general and overall requirements for the project.

**Initial Design Phase**. After analysis of the requirements are completed, the initial high-level design of the overall architecture of the system is created. In addition, the technology and tools to be used are decided in this phase. Apart from the architecture design, user interfaces are also designed in conjunction with the system and database design. These designs are created using the artifacts that are class diagrams and sequence diagrams (Prenner et al, 2020).

**Backlog Creation and Prototype Development Phase**. Gaona-Cuevas, Guerrero and Vera-Rivera (2024) explains that a product backlog is a prioritized list of all tasks, features, and requirements necessary to complete a project. This product backlog comes from the requirements that are transferred from other artifacts, such as specifications, for the agile development phase (Prenner et al, 2020). A low fidelity prototype, solely focusing on the user interface is developed in this phase. This is to give a sense of tangible idea for the stakeholders, so that the solutions are no longer ambiguous.

**Agile Development Phase**. The core development of the project is done within this phase. The implementation of the requirements is done using the agile methodology that is done in iterations. An iteration first starts with the meeting plan, where a subset of features for the iteration and the requirements are divided into smaller tasks to start development. During the execution phase of an iteration, each detailed design of a feature is created and implemented, subsequently, integrations and unit testings are conducted. At the end of an iteration, the increment is presented to the stakeholders in a review meeting (Prenner et al, 2020). These iterations are continuously conducted until all features and solutions are satisfactory to the stakeholders.

**Testing Phase**. The following phase focuses more on the system-level verification tests, since the tests done during the development phase is mostly on unit testing alone (Prenner et al, 2020). These tests include acceptance testings like User Acceptance Testing (UAT) and User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ), integration testings and end-to-end testing.

**Operations Phase**. Finally, the last phase is where the software is planned to be deployed so that the users get access to the software. In addition, all needed documentation is created and prepared, and if needed, the user will obtain training for the software (Prenner et al, 2020).

## Technology Used Description

The development of the AI Integrated School Management and Communication Portal using RAG for SRIAAWP system was done through the implementation of a stack of multiple technologies used throughout the development.

### Frontend Development

Figure 3.3 Impact of TypeScript on Web Development (Emmani, 2021, p. 1740)

For the frontend development, React UI Library was selected to be used because of its reusable component feature that helps save lines of codes and processing time (Lazuardy and Anggraini, 2022). On top of this, Next.js, a React framework is implemented because of its compatibility with React and the flexibility it has with its file-based routing characteristic, that according to Srivastava S., Shukla, Landge, Srivastava A., and Jindal (2024), revolutionizes development experience by blending simplicity and efficiency. Both Next.js and React is built on the TypeScript language which is a modern JavaScript framework. Emmani (2021) states that one of the most immediate benefits of using TypeScript is the enhanced error detection during the development phase. Figure 3.2 shows the impact of TypeScript enhancements on Web Development. A study conducted by Ball (2019) showed that TypeScript’s type system helps prevent a large portion of common JavaScript errors, making applications more reliable. In addition, included in the Next.js setup, Tailwind CSS was used because it stands out for its high level of customization and flexibility. This enables the creation of unique user interfaces without sacrificing consistency and allows for rapid development and iteration (Nandan, Usha and Mohan, 2024). As for the RAG implementation, this project uses the AI Software Development Kit (SDK) provided by Vercel. RAG provides the Large Language Model (LLM) with specific information relevant to the prompt from the user. Vercel is chosen because it is compatible with Next.js and also acts as the deployment platform for the system (Vercel, n.d.).

### Backend Development

As for the backend development, this project utilizes Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS) which is a cloud service model that automates server-side development. This increases the development work speed because developers can focus on building the front-end features, while the infrastructure management is taken care of by the service provider (Uunonen, 2023). BaaS helps connect the front-end with the back end via application programming interfaces (APIs) and SKDs and provides ready to use tools for back-end development like data management, authentication, cloud storage, and functions (Amanuel, 2022).

Figure 3.4 Supabase architecture (Amanuel, 2022)

The BaaS provider selected for the project is Supabase, and its architecture is illustrated as in Figure 3.4. Supabase is a platform that offers backend services and includes a full database built on relational Postgres. An advantage of using Supabase is that it offers the ability to create a table directly from the Supabase dashboard instead of running SQL queries. Supabase also provides its own authentication service known as Supbase Auth, that makes it easy to implement authentication and authorization into an app because they provide client SKDs and API endpoints to help create and manage users. On top of that, one unique characteristic of Supabase is the Row Level Security (RLS). RLS is combined with Supabase Auth to enable end-to-end security from the browser to the database, and ensures strong protection for the data from malicious actors even when accessed through third-party toolings (Supabase, n.d.).

Moving on, aside from database management, the project also utilizes package management to manage dependencies used in the system. Node.js is used because it has a built-in support for package management using Node Package Manager (npm), which is a tool that comes by default with the initial installation setup of Node.js (Node.js Foundation, n.d). Package managers are important because they help manage the installation, updating, and removal of software packages and dependencies (Duan, 2023). According to Saeidi (2025), npm in particular stands out as a central element in the JavaScript community, because of it hosting more than three million repository of packages that are essential in the development of JavaScript-based applications.

## Hardware Requirement

The specific hardware requirements that client machines are required to match to be able to access the system, are to have at least an Intel Core i5 10th Gen or the equivalent or higher central processing unit. Benchmarks show that compilation speed scales linearly with CPU cores (Vercel, n.d.). Hunt and Thoams (2019) suggest that hardware for developers should be at least one generation ahead of the target user to ensure build and test cycles remain efficient. Thus, while 8GB of Random Access Memory (RAM) is the minimum threshold for Node.js, 16GB is the recommended standard because of larger build.

## Software Requirement

Client-side systems are required to have either Windows 10 or macOS and above with support for modern browsers such as Chrome, Firefox, or Edge. The development and maintenance require the widely used IDE, the Visual Studio Code or anything equivalent to support the source code of the system. A stable and continuous internet connection is recommended to be able to smoothly maintain the access to system.

## Chapter Summary

This chapter has outlined the development methodology and approach chosen for the SRIAAWP School Management and Communication project, which was the WAA hybrid methodology. The chosen approach acts as an intermediate between the waterfall approach and the agile approach. By utilizing the advantages of both approaches, the development of the system will be able to benefit from the structured and flexible methodology. The chapter details the justification as to why this project subsequently chose the WAA hybrid methodology and also a clear and concise description of the technologies used throughout the development life cycle. Adding on to that, to ensure the system runs seamlessly on client’s devices, this chapter also includes the details of the system requirements that consists of all the software and hardware requirements.

# REQUIREMENT ANALYSIS AND DESIGN

## Introduction

This chapter goes in an in-depth examination of SRIAAWP School Management and Communication’s system requirements, and the design methodologies that is employed to convert the identified challenges of SRIAAWP into a technical structured solution. Expanding on the stakeholder’s feedback, surveys and workflow limitations, this chapter defines the functional specifications and non-functional specifications. Moreover, it describes the core architectural framework, database schema, and user interface layout that is the foundation for the development and deployment phases. This includes the use cases, and sequence diagrams to illustrate system behavior. Additionally, this comprehensive documentation offers the guidance for the implementation of and testing phases hereafter, and a more detailed explanation is documented in the Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document shown in Appendix A.

## Requirement Analysis

The requirement analysis phase focused on eliciting pain points and problems faced by stakeholders, to structurally document them to be used as guidance during the development phase. The analysis is obtained from holding meetings with the stakeholder representative Puan Izzah and occasionally the Principal of SRIAAWP, Encik Mohamad Faiz would also join. These findings are formally documented further in the SRS for a detailed explanation of use cases and their respective sequence and activity diagrams.

Figure . Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) for SRIAAWP School Management & Communication System

Figure 4.1 shows the WBS for the SRIAAWP School Management & Communication System, consisting of four main modules. The first module being the standard user management module, followed by the department management module. After that, the stakeholders requested an information dashboard module, ending with the cocurricular record module.

### Functional Requirements

The functional requirements define the specific requirements that the system is supposed to do. Each functional requirements were found during the elicitation of pain points and listed down in Table 4.1 below.

Table 4.1	Functional Requirements for SRIAAWP School Management & Communication System

| Requirements | Description |
| --- | --- |
| FR01 | All users shall be able to create an account to access certain parts of the system. |
| FR02 | Admins shall be able to manage all users and their roles. |
| FR03 | Admins shall be able to manage departments, including the teachers within each department. |
| FR04 | Teachers and Admins shall be able to Upload, View, Edit, and Delete official school documents stored in the system. |
| FR05 | Teachers and Admins shall be able to Create, Edit, and Delete events in the school calendar. |
| FR06 | All users shall be able to View the events in the school calendar. |
| FR07 | Teachers and Admins shall be able to bulk import events to the calendar. |
| FR08 | Teachers and Admins shall be able to generate reports for the events in the calendar. |
| FR09 | All users shall be able to query the AI assistant to find specific information in the system. |
| FR10 | Students shall be able to submit their cocurricular achievements. |
| FR11 | Parents and Students shall be able to view students registered cocurricular information. |
| FR12 | Teachers shall be able to review the achievements submitted by the students. |
| FR13 | Teachers shall be able to update the cocurricular students records. |

### Non-Functional Requirements

Non-functional requirements describe how a system behaves, rather than just what it should do. These focus on the quality of the system, like how fast it runs, how safe it is, and how easy it is to use. According to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (2018), the requirements are separated into Software System Attribute, Performance and Other Requirements.

Table 4.2	Non-Functional Requirements for SRIAAWP School Management & Communication System

| Software System Attributes | Usability The website interface should have a modern look that includes helpful first time user wizards and buttons to assist new users without technical training. |
| --- | --- |
| Software System Attributes | Reliability The system should be available whenever the user needs it, especially during peak busy periods. |
| Software System Attributes | Maintainability The code structure should be written clearly so that future developers can easily maintain the system and fix bugs. |
| Software System Attributes | Portability The system is expected to work perfectly on any device with differing screen sizes like mobile phones, tablets, and desktop computers. |
| Software System Attributes | Compatibility The system is expected to be compatible and work smoothly across all modern web browsers like Google Chrome, Safari, and Microsoft Edge. |
| Performance Requirements | Response Time The system should retrieve pages to load in under 2 seconds and react to any user inputs within 3-5 seconds. |
| Performance Requirements | Throughput The system should be able to handle user traffic at peak periods smoothly like handling 200 parents log in at the same time. |
| Performance Requirements | Capacity The system is expected to have enough storage space to keep years of school information, student records and teacher documents in the database. |
| Performance Requirements | Availability The system aims for a 99% availability rate, to ensure users can access it almost at any time. |
| Other Requirements | Security The system should only authorize logged in users to access certain parts of the system by using Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). |
| Other Requirements | Safety The system must automatically backup files and records in the database on a daily basis to avoid data loss. |
| Other Requirements | Legal and Regulatory The system should get user consent before storing personal data. |
| Other Requirements | Environmental The system is expected to reduce the usage of papers and physical documents because of the digitization of manual processes. |

## Database Design

Figure . Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD) for SRIAAWP Portal

The Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD) illustrates the structure of the SRIAAWP Portal’s Supabase database, which is built on PostgreSQL. It highlights key main tables like PROFILES connected to Supabase Auth’s auth_users, TEACHERS that organizes DEPARTMENTS which has multiple DOCUMENTS, EVENTS that is managed by teachers, ACHIEVEMENTS that are submitted by STUDENTS and reviewed by teachers. It maps out how different entities interact with each other, while maintaining an organized database that does not violate any database principles. Further explanation of each entity is detailed in the SDS document as in Appendix B.

## Chapter Summary

This chapter provided the analysis and design basis for the SRIAAWP School Management and Communication Portal. It starts with analyzing the requirements received from the stakeholders by translating the needs into functional requirements and capabilities, like what features will be included, and also the non-functional criteria like its performance, usability, maintainability, and security. This chapter also describes the use cases for the system and shows the general use case diagram along with the architecture of the system. The database design illustrates the ERD of the system that becomes the foundation for the Supabase database design. Finally, this chapter covers the user interface design to be developed. It illustrates the high fidelity prototype concept for the system.

# CONCLUSION

## Achievement of Project Objectives

For this project on system development, there are a total of three project objectives as stated in chapter 1. The first objective is to analyze the requirements of the stakeholder, SRIAAWP, and the second objective is to design and develop a centralized web application including an administrative dashboard integrated with an AI-powered RAG, and an information dashboard integrated using a conflict-free calendar. In FYP-1, the first objective is completely fulfilled as the problems and pain points faced by the stakeholders are identified specifically throughout chapter 4 and the SRS document as in Appendix A. A detailed explanation on functional and non-functional requirements of the system are further described, and behavioral diagrams like use case diagram, activity diagrams, and sequence diagrams are illustrated in the SRS document aswell. Furthermore, objective two is partially fulfilled, specifically in terms of designing the system to be developed. The system design including its database design like its ERD diagram, and each module’s user interface are further illustrated and described throughout chapter 4 and the SDS document as in Appendix B. This concludes the first phase of the FYP project for this semester.

## Planning for FYP2

For the second phase of the whole FYP project, the development, implementation and testing stage of the AI Integrated School Portal using RAG for SRIAAWP system, will be to achieve the second half of objective two and objective three. Objective two is to start the development of the system, and objective three is to test the overall system with end users. The development will be conducted on the basis of using the technology stack mentioned inside of Chapter 3. This includes the utilization of software like VS Code as the main IDE, Next.js as the framework built on React UI Library, and using Supabase as the backend BaaS. The testing of this project will be conducted along with the foundation set from the Software Test Description (STD) as in Appendix C, and along with the cooperation with the stakeholders. Lastly, the implementation of the system will be as a web application using available online hosting services like Vercel. This service offers an optimized environment for the frontend performance, which is important for the stakeholders.
